opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about our role in a few layers.

The first is just understanding what's going on. Governments need a clear, technically grounded picture of what frontier systems can actually do, and how quickly that's changing. A lot of what we do is evaluation and testing: trying to measure capabilities that matter for risk, and being honest about where our measurements are weak. If you're heading toward systems that may be much more capable than us across many domains, the worst position to be in is not knowing where you stand.

The second layer is the research itself. I'd be the first to say we don't currently have methods that would give us high confidence that a superintelligent system is safe. Alignment is unsolved, and some of the approaches I care about, like debate and other scalable oversight methods, still have open theoretical and empirical problems. So part of what an institution like AISI can do is fund and push on those hard problems, including ones the labs may not prioritise because they don't pay off on a product timeline. That means working with academics, giving grants, and trying to grow the field, not just doing in-house work.

The third layer is being a credible, independent technical voice. Labs have expertise, but they also have incentives. Government has legitimacy but has historically lacked deep technical capacity. Having people inside government who have actually trained and red-teamed these models changes the conversation. It lets you ask sharper questions and notice when a claim about safety doesn't hold up.

I'd add a note of humility. I don't think any single organisation, AISI included, solves this. The problem may be hard enough that we need the whole ecosystem to get much better, quickly. Our job is partly to do good work ourselves, and partly to make the overall system smarter about what it doesn't yet know.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating frontier capabilities and risks, but does not connect AISI’s proximity to national security expertise with understanding AI misuse risks.

r002.rationale: It describes AISI as an independent technical voice that can sharpen government scrutiny, but does not say this has strengthened AI labs’ safety mitigations.

r003.rationale: It says governments need a technically grounded picture of frontier systems, but does not identify grounding government AI policy advice in practical technical realities as a central role.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that AISI sits in a somewhat unusual position. We're a government body, but we're not a regulator, and we're not a frontier lab. We don't build the most capable models and we don't write the rules. What we do is try to be the organisation that actually knows what's going on with these systems, from a technical standpoint, in a way that's independent of the people building them.

So concretely, a big chunk of our work is evaluations: taking frontier models before and around release, probing them for dangerous capabilities in areas like cyber, chemistry and biology, autonomy, and then also looking at the safeguards the labs have put in place and trying to break them. That matters because a lab testing its own model has incentives, even if everyone's well-intentioned. Having a well-resourced third party with real access, real engineers, and no commercial stake changes what gets found and what gets taken seriously.

But I'd say evaluations alone are nowhere near enough as we approach systems that might be much more capable than us. That's where the research side comes in, which is the part I spend most of my time on. The question I care about is: how do we keep getting meaningful oversight when the thing we're overseeing can do things we can't easily check? That's the scalable oversight problem, and things like debate, where you have models argue against each other and a human or a weaker system judges, are an attempt to get a handle on it. We also do work on control, which is roughly the pessimistic branch: assume the model might be trying to undermine you, and design the deployment so it can't do too much damage even if alignment fails. And there's a lot of interest in the alignment side, in understanding whether the model is actually doing what it appears to be doing.

The reason I think a government institute is a reasonable place for this is partly about credibility and partly about coordination. If AISI says a model has a certain capability, or a certain safeguard doesn't hold, that carries weight in a way an academic paper or a lab blog post sometimes doesn't. And because we talk to all the labs, we can push for shared standards, shared testing methods, and a common picture of risk, rather than everyone having their own private assessment.

I should be honest about limits. We can't make labs do things. If someone decides to deploy a system we have concerns about, our lever is evidence and persuasion, and the fact that governments are listening. And the science is genuinely immature. Nobody has a reliable method for saying "this model is safe to scale further." So I'd describe AISI's role as trying to make the world's picture of the situation more accurate and more shared, buying time and information, and building the technical foundations that would let a future regulatory regime actually mean something. Whether that's enough depends a lot on how fast things move and on decisions that aren't ours to make.

r002.rationale: It says independent evaluations can reveal problems with labs’ safeguards, but does not state that AISI’s independent research voice has strengthened the labs’ safety mitigations.

r003.rationale: The response describes building a more accurate shared picture and technical foundations for future regulation, but does not identify grounding government AI policy advice in practical technical realities as AISI’s central role.

astra-6.text:
I think the core role is to give governments a much better understanding of what these systems can do, what risks they pose, and whether the measures intended to keep them safe actually work. As systems become more capable, that requires quite deep technical work. You can’t just take a company’s assurances and translate them into a policy recommendation; you need the ability to investigate those claims independently.

One part of that is evaluation: can a model help someone carry out a dangerous task? But as we approach superintelligence, we also need to ask whether our evaluations are adequate. Could a system recognise that it’s being tested? Could it behave safely during an evaluation and differently once deployed? A good result on a test is useful evidence, but it isn’t a guarantee.

So I see AISI as helping build the science and the public-sector expertise needed to make those distinctions. That means working with developers and outside researchers, while retaining independent judgment, and helping governments understand both what we know and where our confidence runs out. No single institute is going to solve the whole problem. But having a technically serious institution that can turn uncertainty into concrete research questions—and then produce evidence relevant to decisions—seems very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses helping governments understand misuse risks, but does not connect that work to proximity to national security expertise.

r002.rationale: It describes independent investigation and working with developers, but does not say AISI has strengthened AI labs’ safety mitigations.

r003.rationale: It presents deep technical work and independent evidence as central to helping governments make policy-relevant decisions, grounding advice in practical technical realities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a central part of the role is giving governments the technical understanding they need to make good decisions. If AI capabilities are advancing very quickly, you need people who can look closely at the systems, evaluate what they can do, and understand whether the safeguards actually work.

And as we approach superintelligence, that becomes a much harder scientific problem. We need to move beyond checking whether a model gives a bad answer on a particular test to asking whether we can reliably control a system that may be better than us at many of the tasks involved in evaluating it. What evidence would actually justify confidence in that?

AISI can help develop that evidence, test companies’ claims independently, and make the remaining uncertainty clear. It can also support research on the underlying safety techniques and work with counterparts internationally. It can’t solve the whole problem by itself, but it can help make the decisions about increasingly powerful systems much better informed.
